Customers link to a state/province through their delivery city: Sales.Customers.DeliveryCityID → Application.Cities.CityID → Application.StateProvinces.StateProvinceID. I use the delivery city, since it is the main location for a customer. I then group by state province name and count the customers.

```sql
SELECT sp.StateProvinceName,
       COUNT(c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.StateProvinceName
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.StateProvinceName;
```

The question asks for the account name with the earliest opening date, which is the customer with the minimum `AccountOpenedDate` in `Sales.Customers`. I order by that date ascending and take one row. I add `CustomerID` as a tie-breaker so the result is deterministic when several accounts share the date.

```sql
SELECT CustomerName
FROM Sales.Customers
ORDER BY AccountOpenedDate ASC, CustomerID ASC
LIMIT 1;
```

Average transaction amount per customer: group Sales.CustomerTransactions by CustomerID and average TransactionAmount. I'll also join Customers to include the name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

The question doesn't name a table, so I assumed it means customer transactions. In `Sales.CustomerTransactions`, I read "completed successfully" as `IsFinalized = true`. The query averages `TransactionAmount` over those rows.

```sql
SELECT AVG(TransactionAmount) AS average_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
WHERE IsFinalized = true;
```

Quantity sold per stock item is best taken from the invoice lines, since those record what was actually sold. I'll group by stock item, join to StockItems for the name, and average the quantity.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       AVG(il.Quantity) AS average_quantity_sold
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY si.StockItemID;
```

Backorders are identified in Sales.Orders. An order that has a non-null BackorderOrderID has a backorder created for it, so I count the distinct customers on those orders.

An alternative reading is that an order is itself a backorder when some other order points to it through BackorderOrderID. Both readings give the same customers, because the backorder is created for the same customer as the original order. The first reading is simpler, so I use it.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL;
```

The query assumes the following:

- **Black Friday 2024** is the day after US Thanksgiving, which is 2024-11-29.
- **Order value** is the sum of `quantity * unitprice` over an order's lines.
- **An order has a promotion** if at least one of its lines matches a special deal that is active on the order date. A deal matches when the deal's date range covers the order date and every non-null deal criterion fits the line or customer. Those criteria are stock item, customer, buying group, customer category and stock group.

```sql
WITH bf_orders AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           (SELECT SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice)
              FROM Sales.OrderLines ol
             WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID) AS order_value,
           EXISTS (
               SELECT 1
                 FROM Sales.OrderLines ol2
                 JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
                 JOIN Sales.SpecialDeals sd
                   ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
                  AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol2.StockItemID)
                  AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = c.CustomerID)
                  AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
                  AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
                  AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
                         SELECT 1
                           FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
                          WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol2.StockItemID
                            AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
                WHERE ol2.OrderID = o.OrderID
           ) AS has_promotion
      FROM Sales.Orders o
     WHERE o.OrderDate = DATE '2024-11-29'
)
SELECT CASE WHEN has_promotion THEN 'With promotion' ELSE 'Without promotion' END AS promotion_status,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       AVG(order_value) AS average_order_value
  FROM bf_orders
 WHERE order_value IS NOT NULL
 GROUP BY has_promotion
 ORDER BY has_promotion DESC;
```

Backorders are identified by Sales.Orders.BackorderOrderID being not null (the order that has a backorder created). Count distinct customers per year of order date, for 2000–2020.

Alternatively, IsUndersupplyBackordered could be used, but a non-null BackorderOrderID is the more direct signal that a backorder actually exists. I'll go with that.

Years with no backorders would be omitted unless I generate the series, so I'll use generate_series and a left join to show every year from 2000 to 2020.

```sql
SELECT y.year,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM generate_series(2000, 2020) AS y(year)
LEFT JOIN Sales.Orders o
       ON EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.OrderDate) = y.year
      AND o.BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY y.year
ORDER BY y.year;
```

"Stock count" most plausibly means the quantity on hand, summed per brand. That comes from joining StockItems to StockItemHoldings and summing QuantityOnHand. Brand can be NULL, so I exclude those rows.

```sql
SELECT si.Brand, SUM(h.QuantityOnHand) AS total_stock
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemHoldings h ON h.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
WHERE si.Brand IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY si.Brand
ORDER BY total_stock DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Revenue is best measured from invoice lines: the sum of ExtendedPrice (which includes tax) for invoices dated 2013-01-01 through 2013-03-31. Excluding tax would be ExtendedPrice minus TaxAmount, which equals Quantity*UnitPrice. Revenue is conventionally reported before tax, so I'll use that.

Credit notes should be considered, but in WWI the invoice lines for credit notes would carry negative quantities, so a plain sum handles them.

```sql
SELECT SUM(il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount) AS total_revenue
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2013-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2013-04-01';
```

Approach: Find invoice lines for stock items with Brand = 'Northwind', join to invoices and customers, and sum quantity per customer. The customer with the highest total quantity is the biggest consumer. I'm using Quantity as the measure of consumption and the invoice's CustomerID, with the customer name coming from Sales.Customers.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
WHERE si.Brand = 'Northwind'
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Sales.Orders has an OrderDate column of type date, so I filter on 2013-11-01 and return every column.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE OrderDate = DATE '2013-11-01'
ORDER BY OrderID;
```

Order value = sum of order line quantity × unit price per order. I compute this per order first, then average it by customer category, so the average is per order rather than per line.

```sql
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           o.CustomerID,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    GROUP BY o.OrderID, o.CustomerID
)
SELECT cc.CustomerCategoryName,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       AVG(ot.order_value) AS average_order_value
FROM order_totals ot
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ot.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.CustomerCategories cc ON cc.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID
GROUP BY cc.CustomerCategoryName
ORDER BY average_order_value DESC;
```

Delay is the gap between the expected delivery date (Sales.Orders.ExpectedDeliveryDate) and the actual confirmed delivery time (Sales.Invoices.ConfirmedDeliveryTime). I'll join invoices to orders, then to customers and cities, using the customer's delivery city. I'll average the delay per city and take the 5 highest.

Delay in days = ConfirmedDeliveryTime::date − ExpectedDeliveryDate. I'm ranking by average delay, and only counting invoices that have a confirmed delivery time.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName,
       AVG(i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime::date - o.ExpectedDeliveryDate) AS avg_delay_days
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON i.OrderID = o.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers cu ON i.CustomerID = cu.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities c ON cu.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
WHERE i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY avg_delay_days DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Ratio of salespeople to employees in Application.People. The question is ambiguous about whether the denominator includes all people or only employees. "Salesmen to employees" suggests the count of salespersons divided by the count of employees (IsEmployee = true).

In the WWI data, all salespersons are also employees, so I'll count salespersons among employees as the numerator and employees as the denominator.

```sql
SELECT
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsSalesperson)::numeric
  / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsEmployee), 0) AS salesperson_to_employee_ratio
FROM Application.People;
```

The schema has no explicit discount column on orders or invoices. I treated a purchase as discounted when an invoice line's `UnitPrice` is below the stock item's list `UnitPrice`. I counted distinct customers with at least one such line on an invoice dated in 2024.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT i.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2025-01-01'
  AND il.UnitPrice < si.UnitPrice;
```

Interpretation: "items sold" by supplier means the quantity of the supplier's stock items that were sold to customers. Sales are recorded in Sales.InvoiceLines, which link to Warehouse.StockItems (and its SupplierID), which link to Purchasing.Suppliers.

Steps:
1. Join InvoiceLines to StockItems on StockItemID.
2. Join StockItems to Suppliers on SupplierID.
3. Sum InvoiceLines.Quantity per supplier.
4. Order descending and take the top 5.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = si.SupplierID
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_items_sold DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The question asks for the average unit price of stock items grouped by size. `Warehouse.StockItems` has both `Size` and `UnitPrice`, so there's no need for a join. Items with a NULL size will be grouped together as their own row.

```sql
SELECT Size, AVG(UnitPrice) AS average_unit_price
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
GROUP BY Size;
```

The only vehicle-related data is in `Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures`, which has a `VehicleRegistration` column. Each vehicle is identified by its registration, and the table has many temperature readings per vehicle. To count vehicles I need the number of distinct registrations, not the number of rows.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT VehicleRegistration) AS number_of_vehicles
FROM Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures;
```

Stock items have a TaxRate column that is NOT NULL, so "no tax rate attached" most plausibly means a rate of 0. "In stock" most plausibly means the item has a holding with QuantityOnHand > 0. I'll join the holdings table to the items and count the items that meet both conditions.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS item_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemHoldings h ON h.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
WHERE h.QuantityOnHand > 0
  AND (si.TaxRate IS NULL OR si.TaxRate = 0);
```

Stock items store their search terms as a JSON array in the `Tags` column. I expanded that array into one row per term, counted how many stock items carry each term, and took the six most frequent.

```sql
SELECT term AS search_term, COUNT(*) AS item_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si,
     LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(si.Tags::jsonb) AS term
WHERE si.Tags IS NOT NULL AND si.Tags <> ''
GROUP BY term
ORDER BY item_count DESC, term
LIMIT 6;
```

Suppliers have a DeliveryCityID that links to Application.Cities. To find the top 5 cities by supplier count, I join the two tables, group by city, count suppliers, sort descending, and limit to 5. I group by CityID as well as CityName so that distinct cities sharing a name aren't merged.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName, COUNT(*) AS supplier_count
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers s
JOIN Application.Cities c ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY supplier_count DESC, c.CityName
LIMIT 5;
```

Interpretation: for each city that has suppliers (using the delivery city), compute the city's population divided by the number of suppliers there, then return the 5 highest ratios.

Steps:
1. Join Purchasing.Suppliers to Application.Cities on DeliveryCityID = CityID.
2. Group by city and count suppliers.
3. Divide LatestRecordedPopulation by the supplier count.
4. Order descending and limit to 5.

```sql
SELECT c.CityID,
       c.CityName,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation,
       COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS supplier_count,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation::numeric / COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS population_to_supplier_ratio
FROM Application.Cities c
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
WHERE c.LatestRecordedPopulation IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName, c.LatestRecordedPopulation
ORDER BY population_to_supplier_ratio DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "geographical area a company targets" as the sales territory where the company has the most customers. The query joins each customer's delivery city to its state/province, takes the sales territory from there, counts customers per territory, and returns the top 3.

```sql
SELECT sp.SalesTerritory,
       COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.SalesTerritory
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.SalesTerritory
LIMIT 3;
```

Approach: "North America" matches `Application.Countries.Continent`. I link each invoice line to its customer's delivery city, then to the state/province and country. Best sellers are ranked by total quantity sold, limited to the top 4.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON ci.CityID = c.DeliveryCityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON sp.StateProvinceID = ci.StateProvinceID
JOIN Application.Countries co ON co.CountryID = sp.CountryID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE co.Continent = 'North America'
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY total_quantity_sold DESC
LIMIT 4;
```

Interpretation: "items ordered" means the total quantity on order lines, so I sum `Quantity` from `Sales.OrderLines` per order date, using `Sales.Orders` for the date. Then I take the day with the highest total.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderDate, SUM(ol.Quantity) AS total_items
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
GROUP BY o.OrderDate
ORDER BY total_items DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

The schema has no direct link between a special deal and the sales it produced. So I measured a deal's success as the total invoice revenue (`ExtendedPrice`) from invoice lines that fall under it. A line counts when:

- the invoice date is within the deal's start and end dates;
- the customer matches the deal's customer, buying group and customer category, where each is checked only if the deal sets it;
- the line's stock item or stock group matches, where each is checked only if the deal sets it.

I take the deal with the highest total. I haven't run this against the data.

```sql
SELECT sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       SUM(il.ExtendedPrice) AS total_revenue
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals sd
JOIN Sales.Invoices i
  ON i.InvoiceDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
JOIN Sales.Customers c
  ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il
  ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
WHERE (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = c.CustomerID)
  AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
  AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
  AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = il.StockItemID)
  AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
        WHERE sisg.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
          AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
GROUP BY sd.SpecialDealID, sd.DealDescription
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Sale transactions are best represented by Sales.CustomerTransactions (each row is a customer transaction, with TransactionDate). I'll count transactions per calendar month (year and month together) and return the top one.

Considerations:
- Grouping by year-month, since months across years are distinct periods.
- Ties: ordering by count descending, then month, with LIMIT 1.

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)::date AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS transaction_count
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)
ORDER BY transaction_count DESC, month
LIMIT 1;
```

Count the orders per customer in Sales.Orders, then keep only customers with more than 130 orders. Joining to Sales.Customers gives the customer names.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
HAVING COUNT(o.OrderID) > 130
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

The table Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures holds the cold room readings. The question asks for the timestamp and temperature values, so I select RecordedWhen and Temperature and order by time.

```sql
SELECT RecordedWhen, Temperature
FROM Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures
ORDER BY RecordedWhen;
```

Orders link to customers via CustomerID, and customers link to buying groups via BuyingGroupID. Joining Orders → Customers → BuyingGroups and grouping by buying group gives the count of orders per group. An inner join to BuyingGroups restricts the result to customers that belong to a buying group, which is what "each buying group" asks for.

```sql
SELECT bg.BuyingGroupID,
       bg.BuyingGroupName,
       COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.BuyingGroups bg
LEFT JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.BuyingGroupID = bg.BuyingGroupID
LEFT JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY bg.BuyingGroupID, bg.BuyingGroupName
ORDER BY bg.BuyingGroupID;
```

Invoices are in Sales.Invoices, and InvoiceDate is a date column. May 2014 runs from 2014-05-01 up to but not including 2014-06-01, so I filter with a half-open range.

```sql
SELECT InvoiceID, CustomerID, InvoiceDate
FROM Sales.Invoices
WHERE InvoiceDate >= DATE '2014-05-01'
  AND InvoiceDate < DATE '2014-06-01'
ORDER BY InvoiceDate, InvoiceID;
```

Interpretation: the question doesn't say whether "purchases" means orders or supplier invoices. I took it to mean purchase orders placed in 2014, valued at ordered outers × expected unit price per outer, totalled per supplier. If you meant invoiced amounts, the query would need `Purchasing.SupplierTransactions` instead.

Steps:
1. Join `PurchaseOrders` to `PurchaseOrderLines` and to `Suppliers`.
2. Keep orders with an `OrderDate` in 2014.
3. Sum `OrderedOuters * ExpectedUnitPricePerOuter` for each supplier.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       2014 AS PurchaseYear,
       SUM(pol.OrderedOuters * pol.ExpectedUnitPricePerOuter) AS TotalPurchases
FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrders po
JOIN Purchasing.PurchaseOrderLines pol ON pol.PurchaseOrderID = po.PurchaseOrderID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = po.SupplierID
WHERE po.OrderDate >= DATE '2014-01-01'
  AND po.OrderDate < DATE '2015-01-01'
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY TotalPurchases DESC;
```

Monthly summary: truncate the invoice date to month, then sum the chiller and dry items together.

The question says "grouped by invoice date" while also asking for a monthly summary. I'm treating it as grouping by month of InvoiceDate.

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)::date AS invoice_month,
       SUM(TotalChillerItems) AS total_chiller_items,
       SUM(TotalDryItems) AS total_dry_items,
       SUM(TotalChillerItems + TotalDryItems) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.Invoices
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)
ORDER BY invoice_month;
```

The question asks for order details with customer names. I'll join Sales.Orders to Sales.Customers for the customer name, and include Sales.OrderLines for the line-level details.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       c.CustomerName,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.ExpectedDeliveryDate,
       o.CustomerPurchaseOrderNumber,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.PackageTypeID,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity,
       ol.PickingCompletedWhen
FROM Sales.Orders AS o
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.OrderLines AS ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
ORDER BY o.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

The question asks for the total discount amount for each deal description, which is held in the `Sales.SpecialDeals` table (`DealDescription`, `DiscountAmount`). I group by `DealDescription` and sum `DiscountAmount`. Rows where `DiscountAmount` is NULL are ignored by `SUM`, so deals that are percentage-based will show NULL totals.

```sql
SELECT DealDescription,
       SUM(DiscountAmount) AS total_discount_amount
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals
GROUP BY DealDescription;
```

Join the supplier transactions table to the suppliers table on SupplierID to get each supplier's name alongside the transaction details.

```sql
SELECT st.*, s.SupplierName
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions AS st
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers AS s ON st.SupplierID = s.SupplierID;
```

Approach: sum TransactionAmount per customer from Sales.CustomerTransactions, join to Sales.Customers for the name, order by the total descending, and keep the first 100.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       SUM(ct.TransactionAmount) AS total_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY total_transaction_amount DESC
LIMIT 100;
```

Sales.CustomerTransactions has TransactionAmount, which is the amount including tax (AmountExcludingTax + TaxAmount). Grouping by customer and averaging it gives the answer. I join Sales.Customers to include the customer name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS AvgTransactionAmountIncludingTax
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

Order details are the rows in Sales.OrderLines. Each row carries a StockItemID, so joining to Warehouse.StockItems on that column gives the stock item name for every line.

```sql
SELECT ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.OrderID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       ol.Description,
       ol.PackageTypeID,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity,
       ol.PickingCompletedWhen,
       ol.LastEditedBy,
       ol.LastEditedWhen
FROM Sales.OrderLines ol
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
ORDER BY ol.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

Approach: a special deal applies to an order line when the order date falls within the deal's start and end dates. The deal's customer, buying group, customer category, stock item, and stock group restrictions must each either be unset (NULL) or match the order line. The query returns one row per order line per matching deal.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       o.CustomerID,
       o.OrderDate,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       sd.DiscountAmount,
       sd.DiscountPercentage,
       sd.UnitPrice AS DealUnitPrice
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.SpecialDeals sd
  ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
 AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
 AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
 AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
 AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
 AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
        WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
          AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
ORDER BY o.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID, sd.SpecialDealID;
```
